points.slideTitle: Binomial Linnean nomenclature and naming conventions
points.fact: Named according to the binomial Linnean system: genus Escherichia, species coli.

points.slideTitle: Ribosome subunit comparison and storage granules
points.fact: Possesses glycogen granules (inclusion bodies) that serve as nutrient storage areas in the cytoplasm.

points.slideTitle: Medical importance of flagella: UTI pathogenesis and serologic diagnosis
points.fact: Motile bacteria such as E. coli use flagella to propel themselves up the urethra into the bladder, causing urinary tract infections.
The E. coli chromosome (nucleoid) consists of a single circular DNA molecule of approximately 5 × 10⁶ base pairs coding for about 2000 proteins in a haploid cell.

points.slideTitle: F factor, R factors and Hfr
points.fact: The F factor (fertility factor) from E. coli is a conjugative plasmid that carries genes encoding the sex pilus for horizontal transfer of genetic material. An Hfr strain has the plasmid integrated into the chromosome.
Plasmid genes in E. coli encode antibiotic resistance enzymes (such as beta-lactamase) and exotoxins (such as E. coli enterotoxins).
Produces colicins, which are bacteriocin toxic proteins that degrade bacterial cell membranes (by forming pores) or bacterial DNA (by DNAase) in competing bacteria.
Approximately five IS2 insertion sequence elements (transposable elements of ~1000 bp central region flanked by inverted repeats) are found in the chromosome of many E. coli strains.

points.slideTitle: Resistance plasmid functions and host range
points.fact: Carries resistance plasmids (R plasmids) encoding β-lactamases that degrade antibiotics; these can transfer by conjugation to cells of the same or other species.
Has a rapid generation time of approximately 20 minutes under favorable nutritional and incubation conditions.
Ferments lactose, turning phenol red indicator yellow; used diagnostically to differentiate E. coli (lactose fermenter) from Salmonella and Shigella (non-lactose fermenters).

points.slideTitle: Iron metabolism: Ferric ion and siderophores
points.fact: Secretes enterobactin (a siderophore) to capture ferric iron sequestered by host transferrin and transport it into the bacterial cell.
A key resident flora organism of the colon and small intestine; harmless in its normal habitat but causes disease (e.g. UTI) when introduced into the urinary bladder.

points.slideTitle: Table 6-1: Normal flora and anatomic locations
points.fact: Normal flora resident located in the colon, vagina, and outer urethra.
A major facultative anaerobe of the intestinal normal flora colonizing the colon.
Plays a significant role in extra-intestinal disease: E. coli is the leading cause of urinary tract infections when flora ascends into the urinary tract.

points.slideTitle: Summary of diseases caused by normal flora
points.fact: Summary of diseases caused by normal flora: E. coli normal flora causes urinary tract infections (UTI).
Ascending genitourinary flora involvement: E. coli can ascend to cause cystitis and urinary tract infections.
Infection and strain-dependent outcomes: different strains of E. coli produce different exotoxins, leading to distinct clinical syndromes.
Shiga toxin-producing E. coli (STEC) transmission occurs via ingestion of contaminated ground meat, raw milk, and fecal contamination of vegetables, leading to Hemolytic-Uremic Syndrome (HUS).
Escherichia coli O157:H7 is a zoonotic pathogen with cattle as a major animal reservoir; transmitted fecal-orally to cause hemorrhagic colitis.
Uses pili (fimbriae) to attach specifically to human cell surface receptors during mucosal colonization.
Some strains produce curli (extracellular amyloid fibers/fimbriae) that mediate bacterial adhesion and interact with host coagulation proteins.
Severe bloodstream infection by Gram-negative bacteria such as E. coli triggers disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC).
Surface virulence factor: possesses protein pili that cause adherence to host cells (non-antiphagocytic).
Carries pathogenicity islands (distinct genetic clusters acquiring virulence genes via horizontal transfer) that distinguish virulent strains from benign relatives.
Pathogenicity island (PAI) acquisition in E. coli: nonpathogenic strains gain distinct PAIs to become uropathogenic E. coli (UPEC) or diarrheagenic pathotypes.
Plasmid genes in S. aureus encode antibiotic resistance mediated by beta-lactamase.

points.slideTitle: Resistance plasmid functions and host range
points.fact: Carries resistance plasmids (R plasmids) encoding β-lactamases that degrade penicillin antibiotics; transmissible to other staphylococci.
Classified as an opportunistic/potential pathogen: frequently colonizes healthy hosts but causes invasive disease when host barriers are compromised.
Produces multiple virulence determinants (including toxins and tissue-degrading enzymes) that collectively cause damage and invasive pathology.
Severe systemic infection by Gram-positive bacteria such as S. aureus can cause septic shock and trigger disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC).
Produces coagulase, an enzyme that clots plasma and forms fibrin barriers around staphylococcal lesions, as well as spreading enzymes.
Expresses Protein A on its cell wall, which binds to the Fc portion of IgG, preventing opsonization and phagocytosis by neutrophils.
Protein A blocks opsonization: by binding IgG antibodies in the reverse orientation (Fc region), it leaves no Fc handles for phagocyte receptors.
Surface virulence factor: Protein A is an antiphagocytic surface protein that binds the Fc region of IgG.

points.slideTitle: Table 6-1: Normal flora and anatomic locations
points.fact: Normal flora resident located on the nose and skin.
Colonizes the anterior nares (nose) as a primary reservoir in healthy human carriers.

points.slideTitle: Glycocalyx forms, biofilms, and clinical persistence
points.fact: Produces an abundant glycocalyx (slime layer/biofilm) that allows adherence to prosthetic implants, IV catheters, and prosthetic heart valves, protecting it from antibiotics and host defenses.
A prototypical commensal organism that colonizes human skin without harming the host under normal physiological conditions.
Adheres to prosthetic devices and artificial materials via polysaccharide slime/biofilm production.

points.slideTitle: Table 6-1: Normal flora and anatomic locations
points.fact: Major normal flora resident of the skin, nose, and outer urethra.
The predominant bacterial species of the normal skin flora; nonpathogenic on intact skin but an opportunistic pathogen on foreign bodies.
Colonizes the nose as a normal commensal resident of mucosal and epidermal surfaces.
A regular resident of the normal flora of the outer urethra and genitourinary tract.

points.slideTitle: Bacterial classification by shape and morphology
points.fact: Morphologically characterized as lancet-shaped diplococci arranged in pairs.

points.slideTitle: Bacterial capsule composition, serotypes, and anthrax exception
points.fact: Surrounded by a prominent polysaccharide capsule that is antiphagocytic; contains multiple distinct capsular serotypes.
Naturally competent for DNA transformation (Griffith's classic experiment showing uptake of naked exogenous DNA into competent cells).
A potential pathogen colonizing the upper respiratory tract that causes pneumonia, otitis media, and meningitis when host immunity drops.
Capsular polysaccharide is the key virulence determinant; non-encapsulated strains are avirulent.
Obligatory portal of entry: respiratory tract, causing lobar pneumonia and respiratory infections.
Severe pneumococcal bacteremia/sepsis can trigger systemic inflammatory cascade and DIC.
Produces IgA1 protease, an enzyme that cleaves secretory IgA on mucosal surfaces to facilitate colonization.
The polysaccharide capsule covers cell-surface components and prevents C3b opsonization and phagocytosis by neutrophils.
Surface virulence factor: Polysaccharide capsule functions as an antiphagocytic determinant and defines serotype specificity.
Carries pathogenicity islands and genetic determinants contributing to invasiveness and antibiotic resistance.
Found as transient flora in the nasopharynx of healthy children and adults without active disease.
Lysogenic conversion: temperate bacteriophage encodes erythrogenic/pyrogenic exotoxin in lysogenized S. pyogenes, causing scarlet fever.
Produces multiple virulence determinants including M protein, streptolysins, and pyrogenic exotoxins causing diverse clinical diseases.
Obligatory portals: throat (pharyngitis) and skin (impetigo/erysipelas).
Produces spreading factors including hyaluronidase (spreading factor) and streptokinase (fibrinolysin) that dissolve tissue matrices and fibrin clots.
Expresses M protein as its chief virulence factor: protruding fibrillar surface protein that inhibits phagocytosis.
Surface virulence factor: M protein on the cell wall is antiphagocytic and determines group A streptococcal type specificity.
Can transiently colonize the throat in a minority of healthy carriers.

points.slideTitle: Glycocalyx forms, biofilms, and clinical persistence
points.fact: Produces prominent alginate glycocalyx (slime/biofilm) in the respiratory tracts of cystic fibrosis patients, impeding antibiotic penetration and phagocytosis.
Carries plasmids encoding antibiotic resistance enzymes against antipseudomonal agents.
Produces pyocins, specialized bacteriocins lethal to other competing Gram-negative strains.
Environmental opportunistic pathogen capable of colonizing hospitalized patients.
Major opportunistic pathogen causing severe nosocomial infections in immunocompromised, burn, and ventilated patients.
Infects burned skin, respiratory tract, and urinary tract via compromised epithelial portals.
Pseudomonas bacteremia releases endotoxin that can cause septic shock and DIC.
Surface virulence factor: possesses protein pili mediating attachment to epithelial surfaces.
Possesses pathogenicity islands encoding type III secretion systems and virulence effectors.

points.slideTitle: Table 6-1: Normal flora and anatomic locations
points.fact: Present in small numbers as colon normal flora and occasionally transient on skin.

points.slideTitle: Bacterial capsule composition, serotypes, and anthrax exception
points.fact: Unique capsule exception: its capsule is composed of poly-D-glutamic acid (a polypeptide of D-glutamic acid), unlike nearly all other bacteria which have polysaccharide capsules.
Forms durable aerobic bacterial endospores that resist heat, dehydration, and chemical disinfectants, persisting in soil for decades.
Anthrax exotoxin (composed of protective antigen, lethal factor, and edema factor) is encoded by plasmid genes (pXO1).
Surface virulence factor: D-glutamic acid polypeptide capsule is antiphagocytic (capsule is non-polysaccharide).
Produces terminal round endospores giving a classic 'drumstick' appearance; strictly anaerobic spore-former.

points.slideTitle: Medical importance of spores and tetanus
points.fact: Spores in soil or puncture wounds germinate in anaerobic necrotic tissue to produce tetanospasmin exotoxin, causing spastic muscle spasms (tetanus).
Tetanus toxin (tetanospasmin) is encoded by a plasmid.
Obligatory portal: enters through puncture wounds or skin abrasions under anaerobic conditions.
Obligatory portal: gastrointestinal tract via ingestion of preformed botulinum neurotoxin in improperly canned food, causing flaccid paralysis.

points.slideTitle: Bacterial capsule composition, serotypes, and anthrax exception
points.fact: Salmonella typhi possesses a specific capsular polysaccharide known as the Vi (virulence) antigen.

points.slideTitle: Medical importance of flagella: UTI pathogenesis and serologic diagnosis
points.fact: Diagnosis: specific antibodies against flagellar H-antigen proteins are used in diagnostic agglutination tests to identify Salmonella serotypes.
Non-lactose fermenter: does not ferment lactose, producing colorless colonies on MacConkey agar, differentiating it from E. coli.
Classified as a facultative intracellular pathogen: survives and replicates inside host macrophages and reticuloendothelial cells.
Vi capsular antigen and intracellular invasion systems act as key determinants of virulence in typhoid fever.
Can establish a chronic carrier state in the gallbladder, shedding bacteria in feces and urine without clinical symptoms (e.g. Typhoid Mary).
Horizontal transmission occurs via the fecal-oral route through ingestion of contaminated poultry, eggs, water, or food.
Salmonella typhi is a major waterborne pathogen causing typhoid fever via fecally contaminated drinking water.
Obligatory portal: gastrointestinal tract leading to enterocolitis or systemic typhoid bacteremia.
Non-typhoidal Salmonella species are zoonotic pathogens with poultry, cattle, and reptiles as reservoir hosts.
Salmonella strains produce curli fibers mediating cell surface adherence and interaction with host proteins.
Surface virulence factor: Vi capsular polysaccharide in Salmonella typhi is antiphagocytic.
Possesses Salmonella Pathogenicity Islands (SPI-1 and SPI-2) encoding type III secretion systems for intestinal epithelial invasion and macrophage survival.
Non-lactose fermenter: does not ferment lactose, producing pale/colorless colonies on MacConkey agar; non-motile.
Waterborne pathogen: causes bacillary dysentery (bloody diarrhea with mucus) via contaminated water.
Obligatory portal: gastrointestinal tract, causing colonic mucosal invasion and dysentery.
Carries virulence plasmids and pathogenicity islands encoding cellular invasion effectors.

points.slideTitle: Bacteria not visualized by Gram stain and alternative diagnostic approaches
points.fact: Cannot be visualized on a standard Gram stain because its thick, lipid-rich cell wall prevents dye penetration; requires acid-fast staining.

points.slideTitle: Acid-fast bacteria, mycolic acids, and carbolfuchsin stain
points.fact: Acid-fast bacterium: contains high concentrations of mycolic acids in the cell wall; retains carbolfuchsin stain and resists decolorization with acid-alcohol (appears bright red/pink against blue background).

points.slideTitle: Mycobacterial envelope layers: mycolic acid and arabinoglycan
points.fact: Cell envelope architecture: plasma membrane is surrounded by peptidoglycan linked to arabinogalactan, which is covalently esterified to long-chain mycolic acids.
Demonstrated microscopically as slender, acid-fast red/pink bacilli against a methylene blue counterstained background in sputum smears.

points.slideTitle: Ribosome subunit comparison and storage granules
points.fact: Possesses metachromatic/storage granules in the cytoplasm serving as nutrient reserves.
Very slow generation time of approximately 18 hours (compared to 20 minutes for E. coli), requiring weeks for visible colony growth on culture media.
A facultative intracellular pathogen: survives and replicates inside unactivated alveolar macrophages.
Highly communicable respiratory infection transmitted via airborne droplet nuclei from patients with active pulmonary cavitary tuberculosis.
Transmission occurs by inhalation of aerosolized respiratory droplets.
Obligatory portal: respiratory tract (lungs), establishing primary pulmonary tuberculosis.
Mycobacterium bovis is related zoonotic species transmitted via unpasteurized milk causing gastrointestinal tuberculosis.
Causes granulomatous inflammation (caseating granulomas with epithelioid histiocytes, Langhans giant cells, and central caseous necrosis), contrasting with pyogenic bacterial infections.
Classified under facultative intracellular pathogens capable of replicating inside host phagocytes or extracellularly in cavitary lesions.
Intracellular survival mechanism: inhibits phagosome-lysosome fusion inside macrophages, allowing survival within phagosomes.
Related nonpathogenic acid-fast species Mycobacterium smegmatis is found in normal secretions around the external genitalia.
Obligatory portal: respiratory tract (nasopharynx), colonizing the mucosa before bloodstream invasion and meningitis.
Severe meningococcal sepsis (meningococcemia) releases abundant endotoxin (LOS), triggering rapid DIC, petechial/purpuric purpura, and shock (Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome).
Surface virulence factor: Polysaccharide capsule functions as an antiphagocytic determinant and determines meningococcal serogroups (e.g. A, B, C, Y, W-135).
Carried as a transient colonizer of the nasopharynx in asymptomatic human carriers.

points.slideTitle: Pili (fimbriae) adherence virulence and sex pilus conjugation
points.fact: Pili are critical virulence factors mediating adherence to mucosal epithelial cells; mutants that do not form pili are completely nonpathogenic.
Exhibits widespread spontaneous mutations resulting in antibiotic resistance against penicillins and subsequent therapies.
Programmed rearrangements: shifts pilus genes from silent storage sites (pilS) to the active expression site (pilE), producing antigenic variation of pilin and evading antibody immunity.
Vertical transmission occurs during childbirth through the infected birth canal, causing neonatal ophthalmia neonatorum.
Obligatory portal: genital tract via sexual transmission, causing gonorrhea (urethritis, cervicitis, PID).
Pili mediate attachment to non-ciliated mucosal cells of the genitourinary tract.
Produces IgA1 protease that cleaves mucosal secretory IgA, facilitating colonization of mucosal surfaces.
Obligatory portal: gastrointestinal tract via ingestion of contaminated water/food, causing cholera with severe profuse watery 'rice-water' diarrhea.

points.slideTitle: Binomial Linnean nomenclature and naming conventions
points.fact: Nomenclature: The genus Klebsiella uses the suffix '-ella' to honour microbiologist Edwin Klebs.
Plasmid genes encode antibiotic resistance enzymes including beta-lactamases.

points.slideTitle: Resistance plasmid functions and host range
points.fact: Carries transferable R plasmids encoding β-lactamases that confer resistance and spread by conjugation.
Surface virulence factor: possesses a thick antiphagocytic polysaccharide capsule.

points.slideTitle: Medical importance of flagella: UTI pathogenesis and serologic diagnosis
points.fact: Movement: motile Proteus species use flagellar motility to propel themselves up the urethra into the bladder, causing urinary tract infections.

points.slideTitle: Table 6-1: Normal flora and anatomic locations
points.fact: Normal flora resident located in the colon.
Facultative normal intestinal bacterium that can cause extra-intestinal disease when introduced into sterile sites.

points.slideTitle: Summary of diseases caused by normal flora
points.fact: Summary of diseases caused by normal flora: Enterococcus faecalis causes urinary tract infections (UTI) and infective endocarditis.
